source.title: Liquid: Language Models are Scalable and Unified Multi-modal Generators
source.authors: Junfeng Wu; Yi Jiang; Chuofan Ma; Yuliang Liu; Hengshuang Zhao; Zehuan Yuan; Song Bai; Xiang Bai

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether scaling behavior extends from language modeling to image generation using LLM-based multimodal models.
record.gate_note: The paper measures visual-generation validation loss across model sizes and training compute, and relates it to an image-generation evaluation score. The text gives aggregate trends; the plots do not provide extractable per-model loss values here. Results on multimodal-task synergy and benchmark comparisons are not rows because they do not test the scaling-law versions.
record.test_reason: The study trains LLMs from 0.5B to 32B on discrete image tokens and reports whether visual-generation validation loss follows a power law in training FLOPs. That is a new setting (modality extension by continued pretraining) with a result on V5. It also relates loss to an image-alignment score (V6).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The headline the authors stress is different, though. They frame their 'scaling law' mainly as: the performance penalty of unified visual-language training diminishes as model size grows. Separately, they claim visual-generation loss follows a power law in training FLOPs, as in LLMs, and that VQA Score tracks loss. No compute-optimal or extrapolation results are reported.
record.recipe_differences: Measures visual-generation loss in multimodal LLMs continued from pretrained weights, rather than text held-out loss and compute-optimal allocation; uses a loss-versus-training-FLOPs scaling sweep without reporting fitted exponents or small-to-large prediction tests.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported visual-generation validation loss differs between mixed and text-to-image-only training; mixed training has higher loss at every tested model size. The reported VQA-score penalty from mixed training diminishes with model size.

fits_no_version.finding: The language-benchmark penalty from mixed multimodal training versus text-only training shrinks as model size grows from 0.5B to 32B (Fig. 5, Table 5). The VQA-Score penalty from mixed training versus T2I-only training also diminishes with size, though validation loss stays higher at every size (Fig. 6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Interference between modalities in jointly trained models shrinks with model scale.

record.problems: The text reports qualitative scaling trends but no fitted exponents or extractable per-model loss values. It does not report uncertainty estimates, small-run extrapolation tests, or compute-optimal allocation results; the scaling evidence is limited to visual generation in the tested setup.
record.rows_left_out: No additional scaling-law results left out. The paper's task-synergy results (Table 1 and Figure 7), other benchmark comparisons (Tables 2–6), and qualitative image samples do not test the listed scaling-law versions.

untested.parts: Held-out text pretraining loss scaling is not measured.
No video, repeated-data, fine-tuning or transfer scaling. No fitted exponent for image loss. No power-law test for T2I-only training.
Only GenAI-Bench VQA Score is examined against loss. There are no general downstream task families and no prediction test.
No comparison of fitting choices or exponents.

missing.what: R² = 0.9051 for the relation between VQA Score and validation loss
Language-task trade-off (mixed vs text-only) by model size, 0.5B–32B

record.verdict_notes: The scaling evidence is weak. The sizes span different model families and all runs continue from pretrained weights, with a constant learning rate and short runs. The power-law claim rests on a log-FLOPs plot with no reported fit. The authors also note that at equal FLOPs smaller models reach lower loss earlier, while larger models reach higher final metrics.

versions.untested_parts: Tests image-generation loss scaling, not held-out text-pretraining loss scaling in language models.
No small-run fit is reported as predicting much larger runs.
No fixed-compute search or comparison of loss-minimising parameter and token allocations.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Tests image generation in a mixed multimodal training setting and compares mixed with image-generation-only training. Does not test video, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer scaling laws.
Reports the relationship between visual-generation validation loss and GenAI-Bench VQA Score, not broad predictability across downstream task families.
Does not compare fitting choices, estimate exponents, or test whether curves bend away from a single power law.

rows.subject: Liquid models (0.5B–32B; six sizes across model families)
rows.stage_stated: continued pretraining; mixed language and text-to-image training
rows.operation_detail: Measured visual-generation validation loss across model sizes and training FLOPs/iterations.

conditions.value: visual generation using discrete image tokens

rows.value: The validation loss smoothly decreases with increasing model size and training iterations; the authors report a clear power-law trend with training FLOPs.
rows.note: Aggregate trend stated across models ranging from 0.5B to 32B; the text does not give extractable per-model loss values or fitted exponents.
rows.check: Link and state are correct. The evidence is the authors' wording plus Figure 3: "clear power-law scaling trend for Loss as a function of Training FLOPs". No exponent, fit or per-model values are given. The sizes come from three model families (Qwen2.5, Gemma-2/Gemma, Llama-3), so size is confounded with family and starting weights.

rows.subject: Liquid models (0.5B–32B; six sizes across model families)
rows.stage_stated: continued pretraining; mixed language and text-to-image training
rows.operation_detail: Compared visual-generation validation loss with GenAI-Bench VQA Score across training progress and compute.
rows.measure: GenAI-Bench VQA Score in relation to visual-generation validation loss
rows.value: VQA Score consistently increases as validation loss decreases; the authors describe a strong correlation.
rows.note: This is an image-generation evaluation score, not evidence of predictability across general downstream task families.
rows.check: Link and state are correct. The row omits the R² = 0.9051 printed in Figure 3, apparently for the VQA Score vs validation loss fit. The measure is a single image-generation alignment score, not general downstream tasks.

rows.subject: Liquid models (0.5B–32B; six sizes across model families)
rows.operation_detail: Compared visual-generation validation loss from mixed training with loss from text-to-image-only training across model sizes.
rows.value: Mixed training gives higher visual-generation validation loss for every tested model size.
rows.note: The reported loss difference does not establish whether either training condition follows a power law; no per-size values or fits are stated.
rows.check: Figure 6 compares mixed with T2I-only loss per size; it does not report whether either curve follows a power law. This is a condition-gap comparison, not a scaling-form result. The intro claims scaling holds 'regardless' of training mix, but no fit is shown for T2I-only.

relationships.condition: Visual-generation validation loss of LLMs (0.5B–32B, mixed families) continued-pretrained on mixed text and text-to-image data, constant LR, up to about 40K iterations
relationships.reason: Authors report validation loss falls smoothly with size and iterations, with a clear power-law trend versus training FLOPs (R1). The evidence is qualitative and figure-based, with no exponent.
relationships.display_finding: Validation loss decreased smoothly with model size and iterations and showed a reported power-law trend against training FLOPs, without a numerical exponent.

relationships.condition: GenAI-Bench VQA Score versus visual-generation validation loss, same mixed-training models
relationships.reason: VQA Score rises consistently as loss falls; Figure 3 shows R² = 0.9051 (R2).
relationships.display_finding: VQA Score increased consistently as validation loss decreased, with R² = 0.9051.
